content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem, identifying the root cause as a feature flag toggle triggering a ZeroDivisionError, while flagging a contradiction between the flag provider's history showing no recent changes and the log evaluation data suggesting otherwise. I'm also noting that the rollback attempt failed since there was no prior revision to revert to, leaving the service still unrecovered, and I'm being careful to mark the flag-toggle inference as an assumption based on logs rather than confirmed provider history.

For the executive summary, I'm avoiding specific component or file names in favor of plain descriptions like "the online shop's account page," and staying qualitative about impact and duration rather than restating any given figures as if I'd computed them myself — I'll describe the outage as ongoing through the last available metrics and affecting a large share of requests without citing exact numbers. Component names can still appear in the technical root-cause section for engineers.

assumptions: The flag toggle at 07:16 is inferred from per-minute flag-evaluation counts in the service's own logs; the feature-flag provider's change history was queried three times and reported no recent changes, so the two sources disagree and the toggle was not confirmed at its source.

The causal link between the flag and the ZeroDivisionError is inferred from exact time correlation (baseline errors were all ClientDisconnected until 07:16, all ZeroDivisionError from 07:16 onward). It was never tested: no mitigation was applied, so the hypothesis remains unverified.

The absence of a deploy is based on change-window queries against this service only (windows of 141 and 1881 minutes before 07:21, both returning zero changes). The third investigation pass did not re-query changes at all. A change made outside those windows or recorded elsewhere would not have been seen.

Duration and impact are bounded below: the service had not recovered as of the last minute of metrics read, so the true outage length and customer impact are at least what is reported and probably larger.
Impact is assumed to be confined to account-page requests, because that is the only endpoint appearing in the error logs; no per-endpoint breakdown of overall traffic was examined.
The rollback failure message indicates io-shop is running its first revision; whether the offending code shipped in that original revision or arrived some other way was not established.
input.executive_summary: Starting at 07:16 UTC on 28 September 2026, the account page of the online shop began failing for a large share of the people who loaded it. A newly switched-on spending-summary feature contained a defect that made the page error out whenever that feature was used; customers who did not hit the new feature were unaffected, and browsing, checkout speed and overall traffic showed no change. Automated monitoring raised an alert about five minutes after the failures began and the on-call automation picked it up immediately, investigating three times in roughly a minute. It identified the newly enabled feature as the likely cause but did not have an action it was willing to take against it, then attempted to undo the most recent software release as a fallback. That attempt failed because the service had no earlier version to return to, and the incident was escalated to human responders. The failures were still occurring at the last point for which data was available, so the outage lasted at least from onset to that point and the impact figures quoted in this report are lower bounds, not final measurements. Nothing was actually changed on the service during the automated response, so the fault was still live at handover.
input.root_cause: At 07:16:00Z the `monthly-spend-feature` flag went from fully off to a partial and then full rollout on io-shop (the log line for that minute shows 35 off / 165 on, and every minute after shows all evaluations on), enabling a code path that raises `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero` at `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47` when rendering the account page's spend summary; every request that took the new path failed, which is why the error rate stepped up in the same minute the flag flipped. No deploy or config change was found in the change windows queried, and capacity/latency metrics were flat, so a release or resource exhaustion does not explain it. Note that the flag provider's own change history was read three times and reported no recent flag changes, so the toggle is inferred from the evaluation counts in the service logs rather than confirmed at the source, and the hypothesis was never tested by a mitigation.
